question: Which ATT&CK techniques correspond to the CAPEC attack patterns that can precede CAPEC-691, Spoof Open-Source Software Metadata?

answer.headline: Gathered 3 record(s) from 2 source(s); 2 cross-source correlation(s) on shared identifiers.
answer.narrative: Found 1 CAPEC record(s) for CAPEC-691; ATT&CK mappings: T1195.001, T1195.002. CAPEC-691 (Spoof Open-Source Software Metadata): An adversary spoofs open-source software metadata in an attempt to masquerade malicious software as popular, maintained, and trusted. CAPEC-691 (Spoof Open-Source Software Metadata) has Abstraction: Standard; Likelihood_Of_Attack: Medium; Status: Stable; Typical_Severity: High. CAPEC-691 (Spoof Open-Source Software Metadata) Likelihood Of Attack: Medium. CAPEC-691 (Spoof Open-Source Software Metadata) has 2 ATT&CK mappings: T1195.001, T1195.002. Found 2 record(s) in MITRE ATT&CK including T1195.001, T1195.002. T1195.001 (Compromise Software Dependencies and Development Tools) has 1 technique: T1195. T1195.001 (Compromise Software Dependencies and Development Tools) has 1 tactic: TA0001. T1195.002 (Compromise Software Supply Chain) has 1 technique: T1195. T1195.002 (Compromise Software Supply Chain) has 1 tactic: TA0001. 2 identifiers are corroborated across both CAPEC and ATT&CK (T1195.001, T1195.002).

results.sub_question: Retrieve the Technique and SubTechnique nodes whose attack_id matches the ATT&CK technique ids (e.g. T1234, T1234.001) returned by the CAPEC TaxonomyEntry results from q1. Return the technique name, id, and any associated Tactic via HAS_TACTIC.
results.query: MATCH (n) WHERE coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (n)<-[:HAS_SUBTECHNIQUE]-(m0) WHERE n:SubTechnique OR NOT (n:SubTechnique OR n:Tactic OR n:Technique) WITH n, collect(DISTINCT {m: m0, r: 'HAS_SUBTECHNIQUE'}) AS h0 OPTIONAL MATCH (n)<-[:HAS_TECHNIQUE]-(m1) WHERE n:SubTechnique OR NOT (n:SubTechnique OR n:Tactic OR n:Technique) WITH n, h0, collect(DISTINCT {m: m1, r: 'HAS_TECHNIQUE'}) AS h1 OPTIONAL MATCH (n)-[:HAS_TECHNIQUE]->(m2) WHERE n:Tactic OR NOT (n:SubTechnique OR n:Tactic OR n:Technique) WITH n, h0, h1, collect(DISTINCT {m: m2, r: 'HAS_TECHNIQUE'}) AS h2 OPTIONAL MATCH (n)-[:HAS_SUBTECHNIQUE]->(m3) WHERE n:Technique OR NOT (n:SubTechnique OR n:Tactic OR n:Technique) WITH n, h0, h1, h2, collect(DISTINCT {m: m3, r: 'HAS_SUBTECHNIQUE'}) AS h3 OPTIONAL MATCH (n)<-[:HAS_TECHNIQUE]-(m4) WHERE n:Technique OR NOT (n:SubTechnique OR n:Tactic OR n:Technique) WITH n, h0, h1, h2, h3, collect(DISTINCT {m: m4, r: 'HAS_TECHNIQUE'}) AS h4 OPTIONAL MATCH (n)-[:HAS_SUBTECHNIQUE]->(c0) WHERE n:Technique OR NOT (n:SubTechnique OR n:Tactic OR n:Technique) WITH n, h0, h1, h2, h3, h4, collect(DISTINCT {m: c0, r: 'HAS_SUBTECHNIQUE'}) AS k0 OPTIONAL MATCH (n)-[:HAS_SUBTECHNIQUE]->(c1v0)<-[:HAS_TECHNIQUE]-(c1) WHERE n:Technique OR NOT (n:SubTechnique OR n:Tactic OR n:Technique) WITH n, h0, h1, h2, h3, h4, k0, collect(DISTINCT {m: c1, r: 'HAS_TECHNIQUE', via: c1v0}) AS k1 WITH n, [x IN k0 + k1 WHERE x.m IS NOT NULL] AS chained, h0 + h1 + h2 + h3 + h4 AS star WITH n, CASE WHEN size(chained) = 0 THEN star ELSE chained END AS hops UNWIND (CASE WHEN size(hops) = 0 THEN [{m: null, r: null}] ELSE hops END) AS hop RETURN coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) AS anchor_id, n.name AS anchor_name, labels(n)[0] AS anchor_label, coalesce(hop.m.attack_id, hop.m.id) AS neighbour_id, hop.m.name AS neighbour_name, labels(hop.m)[0] AS neighbour_label, hop.r AS rel_type, coalesce(hop.via.attack_id, hop.via.id) AS via_id LIMIT 1000

related.name: Supply Chain Compromise
related.label: Technique
related.description:
Adversaries may manipulate products or product delivery mechanisms prior to receipt by a final consumer for the purpose of data or system compromise.

Supply chain compromise can take place at any stage of the supply chain including:

* Manipulation of development tools
* Manipulation of a development environment
* Manipulation of source code repositories (public or private)
* Manipulation of source code in open-source dependencies
* Manipulation of software update/distribution mechanisms
* Compromised/infected system images (removable media infected at the factory)(Citation: IBM Storwize)(Citation: Schneider Electric USB Malware) 
* Replacement of legitimate software with modified versions
* Sales of modified/counterfeit products to legitimate distributors
* Shipment interdiction

While supply chain compromise can impact any component of hardware or software, adversaries looking to gain execution have often focused on malicious additions to legitimate software in software distribution or update channels.(Citation: Avast CCleaner3 2018)(Citation: Microsoft Dofoil 2018)(Citation: Command Five SK 2011) Adversaries may limit targeting to a desired victim set or distribute malicious software to a broad set of consumers but only follow up with specific victims.(Citation: Symantec Elderwood Sept 2012)(Citation: Avast CCleaner3 2018)(Citation: Command Five SK 2011) Popular open-source projects that are used as dependencies in many applications may also be targeted as a means to add malicious code to users of the dependency.(Citation: Trendmicro NPM Compromise)

In some cases, adversaries may conduct “second-order” supply chain compromises by leveraging the access gained from an initial supply chain compromise to further compromise a software component.(Citation: Krebs 3cx overview 2023) This may allow the threat actor to spread to even more victims.

related.name: Initial Access
related.label: Tactic
related.description:
The adversary is trying to get into your network.

Initial Access consists of techniques that use various entry vectors to gain their initial foothold within a network. Techniques used to gain a foothold include targeted spearphishing and exploiting weaknesses on public-facing web servers. Footholds gained through initial access may allow for continued access, like valid accounts and use of external remote services, or may be limited-use due to changing passwords.
